key_insight: Data leakage and evaluation artifacts can substantially inflate apparent rare disease diagnostic performance in augmented LLM systems.
clinical_relevance: High benchmark accuracy alone does not establish reliable diagnostic performance in real-world clinical settings.
method: Audited evaluation artifacts using over 60,000 cases from public and independent clinical cohorts.
Reconstructed an agentic framework and tested strict cross-dataset isolation alongside supervised classifier evaluations.
Examined retrospective treatment cues and temporal misalignment in foundational knowledge bases.
evidence_signal: Strict isolation reduced agentic mean Recall@1 from 54.3% to 40.3% (Hedges’ g = 0.94), while supervised classifier accuracy fell from 42.9% internally to 16.7% across external cohorts (Cohen’s d = 2.01).
watch_item: Real-world clinical utility remains unproven; leakage-controlled benchmarks are necessary but do not substitute for prospective clinical validation.
paper_title: Auditing evaluation artifacts and data leakage in large language model systems for rare disease diagnosis
